title: Smog, Lead and Oil: The Car's Hidden Costs
summary: Cars gave people freedom, but their exhaust carried hidden dangers: poisonous lead, eye-stinging smog and invisible carbon dioxide. Brave scientists tracked down the problems, and new laws and clever inventions like the catalytic converter made the air much cleaner.

sections.heading: A Knock in the Engine
paragraphs: Imagine riding in a shiny new car in about 1920. You press the pedal to climb a hill, and from under the hood comes a sharp, metallic rattle: ping-ping-ping, like someone tapping the engine with a tiny hammer. Drivers called it knock. It was more than an annoying sound. Knock meant the fuel inside the cylinders was exploding at the wrong moment, slamming against the piston instead of pushing it smoothly. It wasted power, overheated engines and, if it went on long enough, could crack or melt parts.

Engineers knew there was a cure for knock in theory. If engines could squeeze the fuel-air mixture harder, they would be more powerful and use less fuel. But the harder you squeezed ordinary gasoline, the more it knocked. So carmakers were stuck building low-compression engines that wasted a lot of their fuel. Whoever found a way to stop knock would unlock cars that were faster, stronger and cheaper to run.

At General Motors, the problem landed on the desk of Charles Kettering, the same inventive engineer whose electric self-starter had ended hand-cranking in 1912. Kettering's research team in Dayton, Ohio, included a young engineer named Thomas Midgley Jr., born in 1889. Midgley was not trained as a chemist, but he was curious, energetic and willing to try almost anything. For several years he and his helpers mixed one substance after another into gasoline, ran it through a test engine and listened.

Some of their attempts sound funny today. Iodine helped a little but was expensive and corroded metal. A compound containing tellurium worked quite well, but it gave off a garlic-like stink so powerful and long-lasting that it clung to the people who handled it. Nobody wanted to buy fuel that made them smell. The team kept searching through the chemical elements, looking for heavy metal compounds that might calm the explosion.

On 9 December 1921, Midgley's team tried a liquid called tetraethyl lead, often shortened to TEL. It is a compound in which a single atom of lead is attached to four small carbon-and-hydrogen groups. A tiny dose, just a few drops in a large tank of gasoline, made the knock vanish. It was cheap to make in bulk, and General Motors could patent its use. To the engineers it looked like a perfect answer.

There was one word the company did not want customers to see: lead. People already knew that lead was poisonous. Painters, plumbers and miners who worked with it often became ill. So when the new fuel went on sale in the early 1920s, it was marketed simply as 'Ethyl'. In 1924 General Motors and Standard Oil of New Jersey created a joint company, the Ethyl Gasoline Corporation, to make and sell it. Gas stations soon advertised Ethyl as the premium fuel for powerful engines.

sections.heading: The Poison in the Pump
paragraphs: Making tetraethyl lead turned out to be far more dangerous than adding it to a fuel tank. In 1924 a series of disasters struck the workers who produced it. At a Standard Oil refinery in New Jersey, men who handled the liquid began acting strangely. Some had terrible nightmares and hallucinations, some trembled and lost their balance, and some became violent or confused. Five workers there died and many more were badly hurt. Newspapers gave the fuel a frightening nickname: 'loony gas'.

It was not only one plant. Workers also fell sick at DuPont's factory in Deepwater, New Jersey, a major site where TEL was manufactured, and at the research labs in Ohio. Counting the different companies involved, about 17 workers died from lead poisoning in the 1920s. Several cities and states briefly banned the sale of leaded gasoline while officials argued about what to do.

Tetraethyl lead is so dangerous because it is a neurotoxin, meaning it damages the nervous system. Unlike many forms of lead, it soaks easily through skin and can cross into the brain. Doctors today know that even small amounts of lead, breathed in or swallowed over many years, can harm memory and learning, and that young children are especially at risk because their brains are still growing.

The companies fought hard to save their product. On 30 October 1924, Thomas Midgley gave a press conference meant to calm the public. In front of reporters he poured tetraethyl lead over his hands and then held a bottle of it under his nose, breathing the vapour for about a minute, to show it was safe. What he did not tell them was that he had already suffered from lead poisoning himself and had taken time off work to recover. It was a dramatic show, but it proved nothing about the long-term risks.

In 1925 the US government held a conference and set up a committee to study the question. Its report found no clear proof of danger to the public at the time, and leaded gasoline went back on sale. For the next forty years, most research on the health effects of lead was paid for by the industry itself. The leading expert, Robert Kehoe, argued that the lead people carried in their bodies was natural and normal, and that no one needed to worry unless there was clear evidence of harm.

So leaded fuel spread around the world. By the middle of the 20th century, almost every car on Earth burned it. Each time a driver pressed the accelerator, a fine mist of lead particles puffed out of the tailpipe and settled onto roads, gardens, playgrounds and into people's lungs. The poison was invisible, and it would take an unusually stubborn scientist to prove how far it had travelled.

sections.heading: The Scientist Who Couldn't Get Clean Air in His Lab
paragraphs: Clair Patterson, born in Iowa in 1922, was not trying to fight pollution at all. He wanted to answer one of the biggest questions in science: how old is the Earth? His plan was to measure tiny amounts of lead in very old rocks and meteorites. Some kinds of lead are slowly made when uranium breaks down, so by measuring the lead carefully you can work out how much time has passed, a bit like reading a clock that started ticking when the planet formed.

There was a maddening problem. Every sample Patterson tested seemed to contain far too much lead. His measurements kept being ruined by contamination: lead from the air, from dust, from glassware, even from his own hands. To fix it, he built one of the world's first 'clean rooms', a lab where the air was filtered, surfaces were scrubbed again and again, and scientists wore special clothing. Using lead from a meteorite that crashed in Arizona long ago, Patterson, using a method developed with his colleague George Tilton, calculated an age for the Earth of 4.55 billion years in 1956. That number has stood the test of time remarkably well.

But Patterson could not stop wondering why lead was everywhere. Where had it all come from? He began measuring lead in seawater, in deep ocean water and in snow. Later he studied ice cores, long tubes of ice drilled out of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, where each layer holds snow from a particular year. The deep, old layers contained only tiny traces of lead. Then, in the layers from recent decades, lead shot upward, rising steeply after tetraethyl lead was added to gasoline.

In 1965 Patterson published a paper arguing that people living in industrial countries carried far more lead in their bodies than humans in earlier ages and that much of it came from car exhaust. This was a direct challenge to Kehoe and the lead industry, who insisted that the levels were natural. Patterson paid a price for speaking out. Several research organisations refused to give him contracts, and in 1971 he was left off a National Research Council panel on lead pollution, even though he was one of the world's leading experts.

He kept going anyway, testifying to lawmakers and collecting more evidence. Other scientists and doctors added to the case, finding links between children's blood lead levels and their health and learning. Slowly the tide turned. In 1973 the US Environmental Protection Agency issued rules to phase down lead in gasoline, starting in 1976, and on 1 January 1996 leaded fuel was banned for road vehicles in the United States. As lead fell from gasoline, the amount of lead in Americans' blood dropped dramatically.

Other countries followed. Japan was the first to ban leaded petrol completely, in 1986. The European Union and the United Kingdom removed it from sale on 1 January 2000. In 2002 the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) launched a partnership to help the remaining countries switch. The last country to sell leaded petrol for cars was Algeria, which stopped in July 2021. On 30 August 2021, UNEP declared that the era of leaded petrol for cars was over worldwide. It estimated that ending it would prevent more than a million early deaths every year. A few small aircraft with piston engines still burn leaded fuel, and regulators are working on replacing it too.

sections.heading: The Day Los Angeles Thought It Was Under Attack
paragraphs: On 26 July 1943, in the middle of World War II, a thick brownish haze rolled over downtown Los Angeles. People's eyes stung and streamed with tears. Their throats burned, and they could barely see a few blocks down the street. Some residents feared the city was being attacked with chemical weapons. It was not an attack. It was something new, and it would come back again and again: smog.

The word smog had been invented decades earlier by mixing 'smoke' and 'fog', to describe the dirty coal-smoke fogs of cities like London. London's worst disaster, the Great Smog of December 1952, was a winter soup of soot and sulfur from millions of coal fires, and it killed thousands of people in just a few days. But the Los Angeles haze was different. It appeared on bright, sunny days, not foggy ones, and the city did not burn much coal. Officials blamed factories, a rubber plant, backyard trash burning and oil refineries. Closing some of them did not make the haze go away.

Geography made things worse. Los Angeles sits in a wide, flat basin with the Pacific Ocean on one side and mountains on the others. A cool ocean current often creates what scientists call an inversion layer: a lid of warmer air sitting on top of cooler air near the ground. Normally warm air near the ground rises and carries pollution away. Under an inversion, the dirty air is trapped like smoke under an upside-down bowl. And by the 1940s, Los Angeles was a city built around cars, with more of them every year.

The scientist who solved the mystery was Arie Haagen-Smit, a Dutch-born chemist at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in Pasadena. Born in Utrecht in 1900, he was an expert on plant chemistry and on the substances that give foods their flavours and smells; he had even studied what makes a pineapple taste like a pineapple. That skill at identifying tiny amounts of chemicals in the air turned out to be exactly what the smog problem needed.

Starting in 1948, Haagen-Smit collected and studied smoggy air. He found that one of its main ingredients was ozone, a form of oxygen with three atoms instead of two, which irritates eyes and lungs and damages plants and rubber. But ozone was not coming straight out of any chimney. In the early 1950s he showed how it was being made right in the sky. Car exhaust contains nitrogen oxides, created when the heat of burning fuel makes nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine, and also unburned bits of fuel called hydrocarbons. When strong sunshine hits this mixture, it sets off a chain of chemical reactions that produce ozone and other irritating chemicals. The sunny weather that made California famous was cooking car exhaust into smog.

This kind of pollution is called photochemical smog, from 'photo', meaning light. Haagen-Smit even recreated it in the lab by shining light on a mix of exhaust-like gases and smelling and measuring what came out. Car companies and oil companies at first did not want to believe him, and some scientists hired by industry tried to prove him wrong. But his experiments held up. In 1968 Governor Ronald Reagan appointed him the first chairman of the California Air Resources Board, the state agency that would become one of the toughest car-pollution regulators in the world.

sections.heading: Cleaning Up the Tailpipe
paragraphs: By the late 1960s, smog was no longer just a Los Angeles problem. Cities across the United States and the world had dirty air, and millions of people were becoming worried about pollution. The first Earth Day, on 22 April 1970, brought millions of Americans out to demonstrate for a cleaner environment. Politicians noticed. On 2 December 1970 the United States created the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and on 31 December 1970 President Richard Nixon signed a major new version of the Clean Air Act.

The 1970 law set a startling goal for the car industry: new cars had to cut the harmful gases coming out of their tailpipes by about 90 percent within a few years. Carmakers protested that it could not be done in time, and deadlines were pushed back more than once. But the pressure forced engineers to find a solution, and the solution turned out to be a clever metal box bolted into the exhaust pipe: the catalytic converter.

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. Inside a catalytic converter is a ceramic block shaped like a honeycomb, with thousands of tiny channels that give it a huge surface area. The walls of those channels are coated with a thin layer of rare, precious metals: platinum, palladium and rhodium. As the hot exhaust gases rush through, they touch these metals, and harmful gases are rearranged into less harmful ones. Poisonous carbon monoxide is turned into carbon dioxide. Unburned hydrocarbons become carbon dioxide and water. In later 'three-way' converters, which American and Canadian cars began using from 1981, nitrogen oxides are also split back into harmless nitrogen and oxygen.

Most new gasoline cars sold in the United States from the 1975 model year on had a catalytic converter. Converters need to be hot to work, roughly 400 degrees Celsius, which is why they are mounted close to the engine and why a car pollutes the most in its first minute or two after a cold start.

There was a catch, and it brings our story back to lead. Lead in the exhaust coats the precious metals inside the converter and ruins them, a problem engineers call 'poisoning' the catalyst. A single tank of leaded fuel could badly damage a converter. So cars with catalytic converters had to run on unleaded gasoline, and they were given narrower fuel filler pipes so the wider nozzles at leaded pumps would not fit. The need to protect converters became one of the strongest reasons to remove lead from gasoline altogether.

Governments also began checking cars already on the road. In many places, cars must pass regular emissions tests, where a machine measures what comes out of the tailpipe or reads the car's computer to make sure the pollution controls are working. Together, these rules made a big difference. According to figures reported from the EPA, since 1970 emissions of carbon monoxide from vehicles and other mobile sources in the US have fallen by more than 80 percent and nitrogen oxides by more than half, even though there are now far more cars driving far more miles. One modern side effect: because converters contain valuable metals, thieves sometimes crawl under parked cars and saw them off.

sections.heading: Lines at the Pump: The Oil Shock of 1973
paragraphs: Pollution was not the only hidden cost of the car. There was also the question of where the fuel came from. By the early 1970s, the United States, Western Europe and Japan were all burning enormous amounts of oil, and a growing share of it came from the Middle East. Gasoline was cheap, and big American cars with huge engines often managed only around 10 to 15 miles per gallon.

In October 1973, war broke out when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. In response to Western support for Israel, the Arab members of OPEC, an organisation of oil-exporting countries, cut their oil production and announced an embargo: they would stop selling oil to the United States, the Netherlands and several other countries. The embargo lasted until March 1974. Within a few months the world price of oil roughly quadrupled, from about 3 dollars a barrel to nearly 12 dollars.

For ordinary drivers, the result was a shock. In the United States, the average price of a gallon of gasoline jumped from about 38.5 cents in May 1973 to about 55 cents a year later. Worse, there often was not enough. Cars lined up for blocks outside gas stations, sometimes waiting for hours, and some stations hung up signs saying they had run out. President Nixon asked gas stations not to sell fuel on Saturday nights and Sundays, some places limited sales to certain days, and people were asked to turn off Christmas lights to save energy.

In Europe, several countries banned driving on Sundays. In the Netherlands, one of the countries targeted by the embargo, the motorways stood empty on those car-free Sundays, and people walked, roller-skated and rode bicycles and even horses down the middle of the highways. Photographs of families strolling along empty motorways became one of the most famous images of the crisis.

The oil shock changed what people wanted to drive. Many buyers switched from heavy 'gas guzzlers' to smaller, more fuel-efficient cars, and the small, well-made cars from Japan and West Germany won millions of new fans, a story told in Part 12. Governments also acted. In 1975 the US Congress passed the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which created fuel economy rules called CAFE, short for Corporate Average Fuel Economy. Each carmaker's new cars had to reach a certain average number of miles per gallon. The first target for cars was 18 miles per gallon in the 1978 model year, rising to 27.5 miles per gallon by 1985. Similar fuel economy and carbon rules now exist in Europe, Japan, China and many other places.

The 1973 crisis taught the world a lesson it has had to relearn several times since: when a country's cars depend almost entirely on one fuel that comes from far away, events on the other side of the world can empty its gas stations.

sections.heading: The Gas You Cannot See or Smell
paragraphs: Even a perfectly tuned car with a brand-new catalytic converter still sends one gas out of its tailpipe in huge amounts: carbon dioxide, or CO2. In fact, the catalytic converter makes more of it, because its whole job is to finish burning the leftovers. Carbon dioxide is not poisonous in the way carbon monoxide or lead are. You breathe it out every few seconds. It has no colour and no smell. For most of the car's history, nobody thought of it as pollution at all.

Here is a puzzle that surprises many people. When you burn one litre of petrol, which weighs only about three quarters of a kilogram, it produces about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide, around three times heavier than the fuel itself. How can that be? The answer is that most of the weight comes from the air. Petrol is made of hydrogen and carbon atoms. When it burns, each carbon atom grabs two oxygen atoms from the air, and oxygen atoms are heavier than carbon atoms. The US Environmental Protection Agency calculates that burning one US gallon of gasoline makes about 8,887 grams of CO2.

Add that up over a year and the numbers grow fast. The EPA estimates that a typical American passenger car, driving about 11,500 miles a year at around 22 miles per gallon, puts out roughly 4.6 tonnes of carbon dioxide every year. That is about as heavy as an adult elephant, released invisibly into the sky one puff at a time. Multiply it by well over a billion vehicles worldwide and you get one of the biggest sources of carbon dioxide on the planet.

Why does that matter? Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. It lets sunlight pass through the atmosphere but traps some of the heat that the Earth gives off, a little like a blanket. A certain amount is natural and keeps our planet warm enough to live on. But since the Industrial Revolution, burning coal, oil and gas has raised the amount of carbon dioxide in the air sharply, and the Earth's average temperature has risen along with it. Scientists link this warming to hotter heatwaves, rising seas and changing weather patterns.

Transport is one of the largest pieces of the puzzle. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that transport produces roughly a fifth to a quarter of the world's energy-related carbon dioxide emissions, and that most of this comes from road vehicles: cars, vans, trucks and buses, rather than ships, trains or planes. Unlike smog or lead, carbon dioxide cannot be cleaned out of the exhaust by a box of precious metals. Burning fuel made of carbon always makes it. The only ways to cut it are to burn less fuel, to use fuels that do not contain fossil carbon, or to stop burning fuel at all.

sections.heading: Dieselgate: When a Car Learned to Cheat
paragraphs: Rules to clean up cars only work if the tests that check them are honest. In 2015 the world discovered that one of the biggest carmakers on Earth had been cheating for years.

Diesel engines, invented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, are very efficient and produce less carbon dioxide per kilometre than many gasoline engines. But they tend to produce more nitrogen oxides, the same gases that help make smog and harm people's lungs. Cleaning nitrogen oxides out of diesel exhaust is difficult and can make a car slightly less powerful or less economical. In the 2000s, Volkswagen advertised its diesel cars as 'clean diesel', and they sold well in Europe and the United States.

Then a small group of researchers decided to check. The International Council on Clean Transportation, a research organisation, paid scientists at West Virginia University to measure the emissions of diesel cars while they were driven on real roads, using portable testing equipment fitted to the cars. In 2013 and 2014 the team found something strange. In the official laboratory tests, Volkswagen's diesels were clean. On ordinary roads, some were pouring out many times the legal limit of nitrogen oxides.

The explanation turned out to be hidden in the cars' computer software. The engine computer could tell when the car was being tested in a lab, for example from the way the steering wheel stayed still while the wheels turned on rollers. During a test, it switched the pollution controls fully on. Out on the road, it turned them down, letting the car emit up to about 40 times the legal limit of nitrogen oxides. A secret system like this is called a 'defeat device', because it defeats the purpose of the test.

In September 2015 the US EPA publicly accused Volkswagen of breaking the Clean Air Act, and the company admitted that about 11 million diesel cars worldwide contained the software, including about 482,000 in the United States. Its chief executive, Martin Winterkorn, resigned within days. In 2017 Volkswagen pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the United States, and several managers and engineers faced prosecution. By 2020 the scandal had cost the company more than 30 billion dollars in fines, settlements, repairs and buying back cars. The press nicknamed it 'Dieselgate'.

The scandal had big consequences. Governments in Europe and elsewhere introduced new tests that measure cars' emissions on real roads, not just in laboratories. Sales of diesel cars in Europe began a long decline. And many people began to ask a bigger question. If even modern engines with clever cleaning systems could not easily meet the rules, maybe the answer was not a cleaner engine at all, but a car with no exhaust pipe.

deepDive: Historians of science often use the leaded gasoline story as a case study in how evidence, money and regulation interact. Several things made the case hard to settle. First, lead's harm is slow and spread out: no single driver or child falls ill from one tank of fuel, but tiny doses across hundreds of millions of people add up. Second, for about four decades nearly all research on lead and health was paid for by the industry, and its leading scientist, Robert Kehoe, argued for what became known as the 'Kehoe paradigm': the burden of proof lay on critics to show clear harm, rather than on industry to show safety. Clair Patterson's ice-core and ocean measurements broke that logic by showing that modern lead levels were far above natural background. Later studies of children by researchers such as Herbert Needleman linked even modest blood lead levels to lower IQ scores and attention problems. Estimates of the total damage remain debated, but they are large: a 2011 study estimated hundreds of millions of lost IQ points worldwide each year while leaded fuel was in use, and UNEP has credited the global phase-out with more than a million fewer premature deaths a year. Some economists have proposed a 'lead-crime hypothesis', linking falling childhood lead exposure to falling violent crime about two decades later; it is an active and contested research area, not a settled fact. The chemistry of smog is also more complex than a single reaction. Sunlight splits nitrogen dioxide into nitric oxide and a free oxygen atom, which joins an oxygen molecule to make ozone. Normally nitric oxide would destroy that ozone again, but hydrocarbons interfere, converting nitric oxide back into nitrogen dioxide without using up ozone, so ozone builds up through the day. That is why smog peaks on hot, sunny afternoons, and why controlling both nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons matters. Finally, the carbon dioxide numbers follow straightforward chemistry: carbon has an atomic mass of 12 and carbon dioxide 44, so each kilogram of carbon burned yields about 3.67 kilograms of CO2. Since petrol is roughly 85 percent carbon by mass and a litre weighs about 0.74 kg, one litre gives roughly 2.3 kg of CO2.
funFact: Thomas Midgley Jr., the engineer who introduced leaded gasoline, later helped develop CFCs, the chemicals that damaged the ozone layer, leading one environmental historian to write that he 'had more adverse impact on the atmosphere than any other single organism in Earth's history.'
